subtype: Approach: choosing office hours and a polite email [Action]
passage: In Jatin's small college town, the professor came in from the city only three days a week, and the local bus was the one way back. Jatin sat on the shop step and typed an email on the phone: "Respected Sir or Madam, I am a second-year student. Could I have fifteen minutes during your office hours on Thursday? I want to ask about the derivations in the fourth chapter." Nitin, waiting for the same bus, read over the shoulder and said the subject line was too plain. Jatin changed it to the chapter number and the word "doubts". On Thursday the notes were in a folder, and the whole talk fit inside the fifteen minutes.

qa.q: How many minutes did Jatin ask for in the email?
qa.a: Jatin asked for fifteen minutes during the office hours on Thursday.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling about taking up the professor's time?
qa.a: Jatin seems careful and a little nervous about asking, so the polite email with a clear topic shows respect for the professor's limited days.

qa.q: What could Jatin try if there is no reply by Wednesday?
qa.a: Jatin could send one short reminder and mention the same topic, because the professor is only in town a few days a week and may have missed the first message.

qa.q: How might Nitin see Jatin's changes to the subject line?
qa.a: Nitin probably sees a clearer request that the professor can understand at a glance and answer more quickly.

grounding: A student in a small town emails for a short office-hours slot, names the topic and brings notes, respecting the professor's time.

subtype: Approach: choosing office hours and a polite email [Action]
passage:
Wei had admired Professor Rafael Ortiz since his first lecture on game theory, which was exactly why she was nervous about bothering him. On Tuesday evening, in the university library in Toronto, she drafted the email three times.
'Dear Professor Ortiz, I'm Wei Chen from your Econ 302 section. I'm stuck on mixed-strategy equilibria, specifically problem 4 of the problem set. Could I have fifteen minutes during your office hours on Thursday? I'll bring my attempt and notes. Thank you for your time.'
She read it once more, cut one apology, and sent it.
He replied within an hour: 'Thursday at 2:15 works.'
On Thursday she arrived at 2:13 with her notebook open to problem 4. He looked at her work, found the mistake in eight minutes, and spent the other seven showing her a trick she hadn't seen in lectures. She left at 2:30 exactly, and wrote 'thank you' on a sticky note she later forgot to give him.

qa.q: What was Wei feeling while drafting the email three times?
qa.a: She was nervous about bothering a professor she admired, and wanted the request to be clear and respectful.

qa.q: What else could Wei do after the meeting?
qa.a: Send a short thank-you email, since the sticky note was forgotten, saying what she now understands.

qa.q: How might the email have looked to Professor Ortiz?
qa.a: It was easy to say yes to: it named the course, the exact problem and the time needed, and promised notes, so he replied within an hour.

grounding: Shows a student emailing a professor for a fifteen-minute office-hours slot, naming the topic and bringing notes, respecting the professor's time.

passage:
The corridor outside the chemistry department was lined with notices under a slow ceiling fan. Payal stood at the one for Dr Menon's office hours: Wednesdays, 3 to 4 p.m. Beside her, Alka read over her shoulder.
'Just go knock now,' Alka said.
'It's Monday. She's teaching.' Payal opened her phone and typed: 'Dear Dr Menon, I'm Payal from second-year B.Sc. I'm confused about reaction mechanisms, especially why the second step is slow in Friday's example. Could I come for fifteen minutes on Wednesday at 3? I'll bring my notes and attempts.'
'That's so formal,' Alka said.
'She has eighty students. I want to be easy to say yes to.'
Dr Menon replied that evening: 'Wednesday 3:00, room 204.' On Wednesday Payal came with her notes, asked her one question, and left at 3:15. Alka was waiting outside with two cups of chai.

qa.q: When are Dr Menon's office hours?
Why did Payal write such a formal email, and how did she feel about asking?
qa.a: She felt a little anxious about taking time from a busy teacher with eighty students, so she wanted to be clear and easy to say yes to.

qa.q: What else could Payal bring to help the fifteen minutes go well?
qa.a: Her attempt at the example, marked where it stops making sense, so Dr Menon can see the exact gap.

qa.q: How does Payal's approach look to Alka?
qa.a: Alka first thinks it is too formal, but sees it get a quick reply and a meeting that ends on time.

grounding: Shows a student emailing to request a fifteen-minute office-hours slot, naming the topic and bringing notes, to respect the professor's time.
